query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: Under intermediate temperature service conditions and moderate strain rates, an initially single-phase HEA undergoes localized stress concentration at specific grain boundaries, triggering in situ nanoscale phase separation (or ordering) that manifests as brittle, intergranular precipitates, thereby reducing toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, single-phase HEA (e.g., CrMnFeCoNi) with uniformly distributed elements and smooth grain boundaries.
generation.intervention: Apply tensile deformation at intermediate temperatures (e.g., 500–700°C) at moderate strain rates to induce localized strain concentration without overall phase transformation.
generation.conditions: Specimens deformed under isothermal conditions with controlled strain rates, followed by rapid quenching to preserve the microstructural state.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale precipitates or ordered clusters forming preferentially at highly stressed grain boundaries, detectable via high-resolution TEM and APT.
generation.mechanism: Localized stress and strain concentration overcome the local thermodynamic stability of the solid solution, driving elemental partitioning and ordering that leads to brittle precipitate formation along GBs.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to undeformed or differently loaded controls, deformed samples will exhibit emergent nanoscale precipitate formation at GBs correlated with a decrease in ductility (e.g., lower fracture strains by an estimated 20–40%) and increased intergranular fracture.
generation.baseline: The same HEA in the undeformed state or deformed under conditions that do not trigger localized ordering (e.g., lower strain or lower intermediate temperature).
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected primarily at intermediate service temperatures and fails to manifest if the temperature is too low (insufficient atomic mobility) or too high (homogenizing diffusion dominates).
generation.uncertainty: The critical stress/strain threshold for nucleation of such precipitates and their exact composition remains uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a series of tensile tests at varying intermediate temperatures and strain rates on the HEA. Use in situ TEM and post-mortem APT to detect any nanoscale ordering or precipitate formation at the GBs.
measurements: Grain boundary chemistry and phase distribution via APT
TEM imaging of grain boundary structure
Stress-strain curves to compare ductility and fracture mode
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no evidence of localized phase separation or nanoscale precipitate formation at grain boundaries is observed under these conditions, or if ductility remains unchanged, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.kind: web:GB segregation engineering to enhance ductility
cited_evidence.text: To evade the fast segregation of principal elements Ni, Cr, and Mn into GBs, we propose to migrate the fast segregation of these elements from GBs to the preexisting precipitates that are enriched with principal embrittling elements, especially for alloys used at intermediate and high temperatures, because intermetallic compounds can deform at high temperatures, although they reduce the ductility of the alloys at room temperature compared with the single-phase alloys. On the basis of the chemical compositions of four possible GB precipitates in the Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 HEA reported by previous studies (see table S1) (, , ), the Cr-rich σ phase absorbs Cr elements, while it repels other element segregation to GBs. Otto et al. found that GBs are rich in Ni and have no obvious segregation of embrittling elements Mn and Cr when Cr-rich σ phases were precipitated at GBs (, ). In addition, without Mn, Ni segregated in σ phase–free GBs is beneficial to GB cohesion. Thus, it is expected that the loss of ductility at intermediate temperatures can be evaded by preexisting precipitation of Cr-rich σ phases that can absorb embrittling Cr elements from GBs and repel other embrittling Ni, Mn ele

We revealed the key mechanism responsible for the loss of the ductility with increasing temperature, a phenomenon widely reported in the single-phase fcc HEAs that are composed of three or more elements of Al, Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, and Ni. SEM of tensioned sample surfaces of single-phase coarse-grained Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 HEA (grain size around 50 μm) suggested that ductility loss is correlated with the intergranular cracking. However, TEM along GBs confirmed that there are no precipitates of secondary phases along GBs. On the basis of APT analysis, we explored that ductility loss is attributed to fast nanosegregation of principal elements Ni, Cr, and Mn separately into GBs, which reduce GB cohesion and promote crack initiation along GBs. We further demonstrated a GB segregation engineering strategy to evade ductility loss by migrating fast segregation of the principal elements from GBs into preexisting Cr-rich secondary phases in an example HEA, i.e., Cr26Mn20Fe20Co20Ni14. Our work not only provides insights into understanding ductility loss but also offers a GB segregation engineering strategy of tailoring strength-ductility-temperature relations in HEAs.

papers.title: Deformation‐induced grain boundary segregation in a powder‐metallurgy ultrafine‐grained MoNbTaTiV refractory high‐entropy alloy
papers.system: Refractory high‐entropy alloy (MoNbTaTiV) produced via mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering
papers.approach: Hot deformation experiments at different temperatures and strain rates to induce dislocation motion and investigate element segregation near grain boundaries
papers.findings: At relatively low deformation temperatures and high strain rates, appreciable component element segregation is observed localized near grain boundaries; as temperature increases and strain rate decreases, segregation diminishes. Observations include grain refinement, high lattice strain, and accumulation of Ta and Mo at GBs.
papers.mechanism: Dislocation movement under stress creates defects and vacancies that promote diffusion and accumulation of multi‐principal elements (e.g. Ta, Mo) near GBs; the interplay of high lattice strain and temperature/strain rate governs the segregation process.

papers.title: Grain boundary decohesion by nanoclustering Ni and Cr separately in CrMnFeCoNi high‐entropy alloys
papers.approach: Atom probe tomography and microstructural analysis during tensile testing at intermediate temperatures to monitor nanosegregation at grain boundaries; comparison between single‐phase samples and modified dual‐phase samples with preexisting Cr-rich precipitates
papers.findings: Fast nanosegregation of principal elements (Ni, Cr, and Mn) at grain boundaries is observed during deformation at intermediate temperatures, correlating with reduced ductility and intergranular crack initiation. In dual-phase alloys with preexisting Cr-rich σ precipitates the embrittling elements are absorbed, thereby mitigating ductility loss under similar conditions.
papers.mechanism: Fast element diffusion induced by deformation leads to nanoclustering of key elements at GBs, reducing grain boundary cohesion and triggering brittle intergranular fracture. The segregation can be redirected into preformed precipitates, thus preserving GB integrity.

papers.title: Mitigating Strain Localization via Stabilized Phase Boundaries for Strengthening Multi‐Principal Element Alloys
papers.system: Multi‐principal element alloys (MPEAs) with controlled BCC/FCC phase boundaries
papers.approach: Designing an enamel‐like microstructure with stabilized nanoscale phase boundaries that promote trans‐phase migration and dislocation‐mediated deformation, evaluated via tensile tests
papers.findings: Incorporation of nanoscale phase boundaries results in more homogeneous strain distribution, enhancing both tensile strength and ductility; the approach overcomes limitations of localized hardening by promoting energy dissipation at crack tips and crack deflection.
papers.mechanism: Stabilized phase boundaries act as barriers that distribute strain uniformly, simultaneously providing crack bridging and deflection to counteract localized stress which could otherwise lead to brittle failure.

papers.title: Effect of serrated grain boundary on tensile and creep properties of a precipitation strengthened high entropy alloy
papers.system: Precipitation‐strengthened high‐entropy alloy produced by selective laser melting, featuring different grain boundary morphologies
papers.approach: Comparison of samples with straight versus serrated grain boundary morphologies through tensile and creep testing at elevated temperatures (650°C), supported by electron microscopy and molecular dynamics simulations
papers.findings: Samples with serrated grain boundaries show significantly improved tensile ductility (3.5× increase) and creep rupture life (up to 400× enhancement) relative to those with straight grain boundaries. Serrated boundaries reduce local strain concentrations and intergranular cracking.
papers.mechanism: Grain boundary morphology influences local strain distribution; serrated GBs deflect cracks and minimize strain localization at triple junctions, reducing the likelihood of brittle intergranular failure.

papers.title: Microstructure and Mechanical Properties of Intergranular Boride Precipitation-Toughened HfMoNbTaTiZr Refractory High‐Entropy Alloy
papers.system: HfMoNbTaTiZr refractory high‐entropy alloy with minor boron addition
papers.approach: Addition of a trace amount of boron to promote intergranular boride (likely (Hf,Zr)B2) precipitation and enhance grain boundary cohesion; assessment via microstructural characterization and mechanical testing
papers.findings: Boride precipitation at grain boundaries markedly increases their hardness and cohesion, leading to improved work hardenability and ductility. The failure mode shifts from predominantly intergranular fracture to transgranular failure.
papers.mechanism: Minor boron addition leads to the formation of intergranular borides that reinforce GB cohesion, thus preventing crack initiation at grain boundaries in contrast to typical brittle effects associated with impurity segregation in conventional alloys.

established: Conventional alloys lose toughness due to impurity/trace element segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitates.

Single-phase high-entropy alloys (HEAs) and refractory HEAs demonstrate suppression of rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic phase formation, yet still exhibit ductility loss or brittleness under certain conditions.
Deformation-induced grain boundary segregation of principal elements can occur driven by high dislocation density and stress fields.

approaches_tried.approach: Hot deformation under varied temperature and strain-rate conditions to induce/reduce segregation
approaches_tried.outcome: Shown that segregation is sensitive to temperature and strain rate; high temperature/low strain-rate conditions mitigate segregation in RHEAs (MoNbTaTiV).

approaches_tried.approach: Grain boundary segregation engineering by introducing preexisting precipitates
approaches_tried.outcome: Redirects fast segregation of embrittling principal elements from GBs into secondary phases, effectively mitigating ductility loss in CrMnFeCoNi HEAs.

approaches_tried.approach: Modification of grain boundary morphology (e.g., serrated boundaries)
approaches_tried.outcome: Serrated GBs lower local strain concentration and delay intergranular cracking, greatly enhancing high-temperature ductility and creep life.

approaches_tried.approach: Incorporation of stable phase boundaries (enamel‐like microstructure)
approaches_tried.outcome: Provides distributed plasticity and reduces strain localization, achieving favorable strength–ductility combinations in MPEAs.

approaches_tried.approach: Minor alloying with boron to induce intergranular boride precipitation
approaches_tried.outcome: Enhanced GB cohesion and transition from intergranular to transgranular fracture in HfMoNbTaTiZr RHEA.

mechanisms: Dislocation-driven diffusion and vacancy formation promoting the segregation of principal elements to grain boundaries.
Nanoclustering of elements (Ni, Cr, Mn) at grain boundaries reduces cohesion, causing decohesion and intergranular crack initiation.
GB segregation engineering redirects embrittling elements into preexisting precipitates to maintain cohesive interfaces.
Grain boundary morphology (e.g., serration) and stabilized phase boundaries distribute strain and mitigate stress concentration.
disagreements: Whether increased temperature and reduced strain rate completely eliminate segregation (as observed in MoNbTaTiV RHEAs) versus the persistent fast segregation at intermediate temperatures in single-phase HEAs like CrMnFeCoNi.
The relative contributions of dislocation-induced segregation versus inherent elemental diffusivity in causing GB decohesion across different HEA compositions.
open_questions: In an initially single-phase HEA, what is the precise threshold (in terms of deformation conditions and microstructural state) that triggers segregation leading to brittle behavior?
How does the controlled migration of principal elements to engineered GB sites compare quantitatively with conventional alloy behavior under identical service conditions?
What are the service (temperature, strain rate) boundaries over which GB segregation-induced brittleness becomes dominant in single-phase HEAs?
Can real-time in situ methods (e.g., atom probe tomography during deformation) decisively capture the transition from cohesive to decohesive grain boundaries in these alloys?
opportunities: Design a controlled experimental study comparing a baseline single-phase HEA with an identical alloy modified by preexisting nanoscale precipitates or altered GB morphology to test the effect on segregation behavior and toughness.

Perform systematic deformation tests at varied temperatures and strain rates in combination with in situ high-resolution characterization (e.g., APT, TEM) to map the conditions under which GB decohesion initiates.
Combine molecular dynamics simulations with experimental observations to delineate the influence of dislocation activity and local strain on the nanosegregation of principal elements.
Explore alloy compositional modifications that intentionally balance the competition between dislocation-assisted segregation and diffusion, targeting optimal toughness in service environments.

directions.direction: Investigate dislocation‐mediated rapid principal element segregation at grain boundaries under extreme deformation conditions.
directions.assessment: Directly addresses the central question by linking dislocation activity under high strain rates and low temperatures to local GB nanosegregation in an initially single‐phase HEA. Well‐supported by prior APT studies (e.g., PMC11407990, PMC6897545) and is experimentally feasible using in situ TEM/atom probe techniques.

directions.direction: Probe the critical strain rate–temperature threshold at which in situ nanoclustering at GBs emerges.
directions.assessment: Targets the parameter window that triggers brittle behavior. The interplay between temperature and strain rate is well supported by evidence (e.g., PMC11407990, PMC6897545) and such systematic variation is experimentally achievable.

directions.direction: Examine the possibility of deformation‐induced local phase separation or nanoscale precipitation at GBs in single‐phase HEAs.
directions.assessment: This direction tests if slight compositional fluctuations under service conditions (even in a single‐phase alloy) may lead to brittle intergranular precipitates. While it builds on conventional alloy behavior, it explores whether similar mechanisms can be activated in HEAs, making it both provocative and falsifiable.

directions.direction: Assess the role of grain boundary morphology evolution (e.g., transition from smooth to straight versus serrated boundaries) in mediating toughness degradation.
directions.assessment: Informed by evidence that serrated GBs distribute strain more uniformly (PMC9848264), this direction tests whether an evolution toward straight, undeformed GBs under service loading correlates with brittle behavior. It distinguishes the mechanism from elemental segregation by focusing on GB structural features.

directions.direction: Modify GB chemistry by introducing benign segregants (or using GB engineering) to mitigate embrittling element accumulation.
directions.type: Composition design and GB segregation engineering
directions.assessment: While promising for mitigating brittleness, this approach alters the intrinsic GB chemistry and may not satisfy the constraint of retaining the compositionally complex alloy in its as‐designed state. Its indirect nature makes it less immediately relevant to establishing the fundamental brittle mechanism.

candidates.hypothesis: In an initially single-phase HEA, severe plastic deformation at relatively low temperatures and high strain rates promotes a dislocation-mediated influx of vacancies that drive rapid nanosegregation of principal alloying elements (e.g., Ta, Mo or Ni, Cr, Mn) at grain boundaries, reducing GB cohesion and triggering intergranular brittle fracture.
candidates.intervention: Subject samples to controlled uniaxial deformation at high strain rates (e.g., >10^−3 s^−1) and relatively low temperatures (e.g., ~300°C) to maximize dislocation density and vacancy formation.

candidates.hypothesis: Under intermediate temperature service conditions and moderate strain rates, an initially single-phase HEA undergoes localized stress concentration at specific grain boundaries, triggering in situ nanoscale phase separation (or ordering) that manifests as brittle, intergranular precipitates, thereby reducing toughness.
candidates.intervention: Apply tensile deformation at intermediate temperatures (e.g., 500–700°C) at moderate strain rates to induce localized strain concentration without overall phase transformation.

candidates.hypothesis: There exists a critical combination of strain rate and temperature in single-phase HEAs such that beyond a threshold, dislocation-driven atomic flux results in fast nanoclustering of specific elements (e.g., Ni, Cr, Mn) at GBs, leading to a marked transition from ductile to brittle behavior.
candidates.intervention: Perform systematic tensile deformation experiments while varying strain rates (from low to high) and temperatures (from room temperature up to intermediate service temperatures around 600°C).

candidates.hypothesis: During service-like deformation, the initially smooth grain boundaries in a single-phase HEA progressively evolve into straighter, less undulated interfaces due to the accumulation of dislocations, leading to localized strain concentration and loss of toughness through intergranular decohesion.
candidates.intervention: Apply cyclic and monotonic tensile loading at elevated temperatures (e.g., ~650°C) to induce microstructural evolution at GBs.

minor_issues: It is not fully established that cyclic or prolonged loading necessarily straightens serrated grain boundaries; the direct link between dislocation accumulation and boundary flattening could use additional support.
fixes: Include or reference more direct microstructural evidence (e.g., from TEM or EBSD) showing that service-like deformation can remove or reduce GB serrations in single-phase HEAs.
evidence_needs: Data on how GB topography evolves after repeated creep/cyclic loading (e.g., measuring boundary serration amplitude over time).
Comparative metallographic studies showing correlation between boundary flattening, dislocation pileups, and intergranular fracture.

minor_issues: The kinetics of nanoscale precipitate formation under intermediate temperatures and moderate strain rates remain uncertain; it is not conclusively shown that local thermodynamics and timescales permit such phase separation in actual service conditions.
fixes: Incorporate thermodynamic models (e.g., CALPHAD) to clarify the temperature/time window for precipitate nucleation under stress.
Estimate or measure diffusion rates needed for the proposed short-range ordering at grain boundaries.
evidence_needs: In situ TEM or synchrotron-based methods to confirm stress-driven precipitation at grain boundaries.
More precise APT or high-resolution TEM data on possible short-range ordered clusters or incipient intermetallic phases formed under relevant test conditions.

minor_issues: The hypothesis posits a sharp threshold for brittle versus ductile behavior; in practice, the transition may be more continuous or depend on multiple factors (e.g., microstructural inhomogeneities) beyond strain rate and temperature.
fixes: Propose a more nuanced or continuous transition model, clarifying whether the ‘critical’ condition is broad or truly discrete.
Include potential effects from microstructure heterogeneity, grain size distribution, and second-phase particles in the discussion.
evidence_needs: Detailed strain-rate–temperature diagram with mechanical property clouds to confirm the existence of a clear demarcation in toughness.
Correlative APT and fractography on samples across the proposed boundary to evaluate whether there is a distinct shift in segregation and fracture mode.

minor_issues: Although demonstrated in refractory high-entropy alloys, it is unclear how broadly this severe plastic deformation–driven vacancy and nanosegregation phenomenon applies to other single-phase HEAs such as CrMnFeCoNi.
fixes: Address whether the mechanism is specific to refractory HEAs or if analogous dislocation/vacancy-driven segregation can be generalized.
Include a robust discussion or preliminary data from non-refractory single-phase HEAs to support the claim of broad relevance.
evidence_needs: Quantitative measures of vacancy concentration at different strain rates and temperatures, correlated with segregation levels and mechanical behavior.
Detailed dislocation (TEM) and chemical (APT/EDS) mapping pre- and post-deformation to verify the postulated link between vacancy generation and localized segregation.
